name: Zoe Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play hand percussion for a well-booked dance company, record rehearsal rhythms and teach four adults. My music degree and twenty-six years of shows help me hear when dancers need a beat held back. I like the pause just before a whole room starts clapping together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that schedule work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner runs the counter at a building-supply shop and our children are grown. We own our flat, have ten months of expenses saved and my pay is high for this kind of musician; several companies work nearby. I use a paper diary and have never used AI.

say: I'd accept **faster date sheets** with paid player hours visible.
I'd say the **drum beat** still follows dancers' feet.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** and partner wage cover a moved show.
My **paid shows and teaching** should continue through a mild change.
do: Confirm **eight paid shows** and four pupils; request written cancellation pay.
Keep **paper diary** and check each new show date with the stage manager.
feel: I feel **calm** while the season and household income stay booked.
S0.quote: A drum beat has to follow the dancers' feet in the room.
fieldNote: Her **high musician pay** and ten-month reserve make one moved dance manageable alongside a regular partner wage.
She **never uses AI** and checks paper dates with the stage manager.

steps.text: Confirm eight paid dance shows and four pupils; request written cancellation pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company a faster date sheet is useful if it still shows the players' paid hours. A drum beat has to follow the dancers' feet in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten months saved and my partner's regular wage cover a moved performance. I expect the paid shows and teaching to continue in this mild picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm the next eight paid shows and four pupil slots and request written cancellation pay. In the first year of this mild change I'll keep my paper diary, checking each new date with the stage manager before reserving it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our booked season. One moved date would be a nuisance, but it would not put the flat at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a dance moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hall moved a dance last spring and the contract paid half the show fee. I still want the next season's cancellation rule in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI scheduler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not used an AI scheduler. The stage manager's signed page and my pencil book agree often enough.

say: I'd ask whether **generated rhythms** will replace paid recordings.
I'd seek **written fees** for live shows and preparation before signing another season.
think: Recordings provide **one sixth** of my own pay.
Our **ten-month reserve** buys search time, but lost fees remain real.
do: Total **rhythm invoices** and request a written six-month paid show schedule.
Seek **extra paid rehearsals** only after orders fall and the company books hours at a written rate; keep current pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely recording-fee shrinkage despite savings.
S1.quote: An open hour is not a paid rehearsal until a manager signs it.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **available hours** from paid work and asks for actual written rehearsal rates.
Her **AI reluctance** remains consistent; a colleague's demonstration is not a new tool trial.

steps.text: Total rhythm invoices and request six-month written paid show schedule
Seek written-rate extra rehearsals only if orders fall and company books them; keep four pupils

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the dance manager whether generated rehearsal rhythms will replace the recordings I sell. I'd want the next live-show fee and preparation hours written down before we sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recordings bring roughly a sixth of my own pay. If orders shrink, ten months saved and several nearby companies give me time to seek more live dates, but the lost sixth is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll total a year's rhythm invoices and ask the manager for a written six-month paid show schedule. In the first year, if recording orders fall, I'll offer the freed recording hours for extra paid rehearsals only if the company books them at a written rate; I will keep my four existing pupils and paper score notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic cut to recording income, even with a good reserve. An open hour is not a paid rehearsal until a manager signs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are extra rehearsals already booked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I won't count suggested rehearsals as income. The manager has to book and pay a real hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a new AI rhythm tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen to a colleague show a new tool on their own music, but I will not put dancers' private rehearsal audio into it. I am not taking an unpaid course to make the company's recordings cheaper.

I'd seek **signed live dates** while the company still books dancers.
think: I expect **one-sixth pay** from recordings to end in 2028.
Further **live-show cuts** are conditional, not my forecast.
do: List **recording income**, seek signed show dates and request actual pension estimate before stopping work.
Seek **posted tutor work** after 2028 live cuts only if degree/teaching qualify, written net after travel replaces losses and buses fit.
Keep **current shows and pupils** until a suitable signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected recording loss with search time.
S2.quote: Ten months saved is not a substitute for knowing the pension amount paid each month.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 recording loss** comes before 2031 playing robots; live cuts remain conditional.
The job needs **posted qualification**, written replacement net after travel, workable buses and signed offer.

steps.text: List recording income; seek signed paid show dates and actual pension estimate
Seek posted percussion-tutor role after live cuts if music degree/teaching qualify and buses fit
Require written net after travel replacing losses; keep shows/pupils until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company that thinking AGI by 2028 could make rehearsal rhythms before a robot plays hand drums. Playing robots follow around 2031, so I want our live dates signed now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the recording orders to end in 2028, costing a sixth of my pay. I do not expect the dance shows to close immediately, but I will not count another company's chair as open until it is posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list recording income, seek signed paid show dates and request an actual pension estimate before discussing a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if live dates also fall, I'll apply for a posted paid community percussion-tutor role only if my music degree and teaching history qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses serve its hours; I'll keep current shows and pupils until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected recording loss, though ten months saved and several local employers give me room to search. A live-show collapse would be a different, worse case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a tutor vacancy now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No tutor job has been offered to me. I would read its current paid posting and hours before I cut a show date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have the pension figure yet. Ten months saved is not a substitute for knowing the pension amount paid each month.

say: I'd price a **beginner drum circle** during the five-year warning.
I'd require **signed costs** for room and insurance before offering places.
think: Ordinary software may cut **rehearsal rhythms before 2031**, ahead of playing robots.
Our **reserve** should not subsidize an underpaid hall class.
do: Offer **drum circle** after signed hire/insurance costs and eight fees cover room/drum-hire/inspection/insurance/cleaning/my teaching/preparation/travel outside paid calls.
Inspect **eight loan drums** and sound levels; defer and refund everyone below eight safe paid places.
Renew **after 2031** only with eight safe fees covering those full costs and written room terms; keep booked work.
feel: I feel **anxious** until real fees cover all class costs.
S3.quote: A full-looking room can still lose money if my teaching hour is forgotten.
fieldNote: The **separate circle** sits outside paid work; its written room charge includes inspected loan drums, alongside insurance, cleaning, teaching/preparation and travel.
The **eight-place floor** requires inspected drums and hearing safety; every deposit is refunded if it fails.

steps.text: Get written room/cost/insurance before deposits; offer circle outside paid calls when eight fees cover all costs
Inspect eight drums and sound levels; defer/refund whole group below eight safe paid places
Renew after 2031 with eight safe fees covering room/drum-hire/inspection/insurance/cleaning/teaching/preparation/travel under written terms
Keep booked paid dance shows and pupils while testing separate circle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the hall that five years to AGI by 2031 lets me price a separate beginner hand-drum circle. Playing robots follow around 2034, and I would not offer places before the room and insurance costs are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cheapen my rehearsal rhythms before 2031. I know how to teach a first pattern, but I won't turn a good reserve into free hall rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll get signed hall hire, cost and insurance terms before deposits for a separate four-week adult drum circle outside booked shows and pupils. Eight adults must prepay enough for room including inspected loan drums, insurance, cleaning, my teaching, preparation and travel; the hall keeper must inspect eight loan drums and safe hearing levels before I count a place. In the first year after 2031 I'll repeat only with those same full-cost eight safe paid places and written terms; if fewer pay or a drum fails without a safe replacement, I'll defer and refund the whole group while keeping current paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious until the class pays its own costs. A full-looking room can still lose money if my teaching hour is forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a loan drum fails inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cracked drum head or an unsafe sound level means that place cannot count. I would refund every deposit if we cannot restore eight safe paid places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the class replace a paid show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the class goes on a free afternoon. I will not replace a signed dance show or a paid pupil with a speculative group.

I'd remind my children **2039 drum robots** follow today's bills.

Our **ten-month reserve** does not prove retirement is funded.

S4.quote: The pension figure, not a birthday, will decide how much work I can leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 gives us time to read actual pension figures and paid show sheets. Hand-drum robots follow around 2039, but bills arrive before that date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still enjoy paid dance and pupil work. Ten months saved and a steady partner wage help now, yet I cannot name a stopping date without the pension amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid show plan. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep booked dance work and pupils; I'll continue the separate drum circle only outside paid calls with eight safe prepaid places covering room including inspected loan drums, insurance, cleaning, my teaching, preparation and travel under signed hall terms. If safe enrollment falls below eight, I'll defer and refund everyone; I'll slow paid work only if the pension and real fees cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end of the decade while today's pay and reserve are sound. The pension figure, not a birthday, will decide how much work I can leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you received a pension statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not received a pension statement. I will read it with my partner before giving up a signed show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only seven safe adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a class has only seven safe paying adults, it waits. Our reserve does not pay an eighth seat or my missing teaching hour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid rhythms could end before another job is open. Signed dance dates, a real pension statement and a posted qualified teaching role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the teacher when a drum circle fills a hall. Eight names on a drum class list are not eight safe paid places.

headlineQuote: Eight names on a drum class list are not eight safe paid places.
portrait: Zoe is a **58-year-old experienced percussionist** with a music degree, partner and grown children.
Her **higher pay**, ten-month reserve and many nearby companies offer time to respond to recording losses.
She **never uses AI** and checks dance schedules in her paper diary.
She offers a **separate drum circle** only with signed hall costs, eight safe full-cost fees and no displaced paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end Zoe's rehearsal-rhythm fees before a replacement post opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed dance dates**, real pension figures and posted qualifying teaching work with written after-travel pay would help.
